stages.title: Musical notes
stages.hook: A piano has 88 keys, yet music uses only seven letter names. How can so few names label so many keys?
explain: Musical notes use the first seven letters of the alphabet: A B C D E F G. After G, the letters start again at A, but higher. The distance from one letter to the next one with the same name is called an octave, and the two notes sound like the same note at different heights.

On a piano the white keys carry the letter names. The black keys are in between. A black key is named from its white neighbour: a sharp (♯) raises a note by one step on the keyboard and a flat (♭) lowers it. So the black key just above C is C♯, which is also D♭.
Computers and synthesisers number notes with MIDI numbers. Middle C is 60, and each key to the right adds 1. So D is 62 (with C♯ at 61 between), and C one octave higher is 72.

example.q: Which MIDI number is the note one octave above middle C (60)?
steps: An octave has twelve keys, counting white and black.
Add 12 to 60.

analogies.home: House numbers repeat the same pattern on each street. Note letters repeat in each octave.
analogies.city: A bus route A to G loops back to A, like the note names.
analogies.music: A piano keyboard is a ladder. Every twelve rungs the names start again.
analogies.nature: Day names repeat every seven days, just like seven note letters repeat.

stages.mnemonic: A B C D E F G, then round again, higher up the tree.
terms: The distance between a note and the next note with the same letter name.
A sign that raises a note by one semitone.
A sign that lowers a note by one semitone.

misc.wrong: The black keys are less important than the white keys.
misc.right: The black keys are full notes too. They give the sharps and flats that complete the twelve notes of the octave.

stages.limits: Some traditions, such as Indian and Arabic music, also use notes in the cracks between piano keys.

questions.why: 60 to 72 is twelve semitones, an octave.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why only seven letter names are enough for a whole piano.
questions.model: The names repeat. After G we start again at A in the next octave, so every note has a letter name and the octave tells how high it is.
questions.why: Notes an octave apart sound alike, so the letters cycle and do not need new names.

panel.q: A friend says C♯ and D♭ are different keys on a piano. What is the best reply?

panel.q: Why do two notes an octave apart sound so similar?
panel.model: The higher note vibrates twice as fast as the lower one, so the sound waves fit together and the notes blend and seem to be the same note.
panel.why: An octave is a 2:1 frequency ratio, which gives a very smooth blend.

panel.q: A synthesiser plays MIDI 69, which is an A. Which MIDI number is the A one octave lower?
panel.why: An octave is 12 semitones, and 69 − 12 = 57. Both are A.

teach.model: Notes use the letters A to G. After G the letters start again at A higher up, and that gap is an octave. Black keys on a piano are sharps and flats, one small step above or below a white key.

stages.title: Staff notation
stages.hook: If you wrote a secret code for sounds, how would you show high and low on paper?
explain: Music is written on a staff, which is five horizontal lines with four spaces. A note placed higher on the staff sounds higher. The note sits either on a line or in a space.

At the start of the staff is a clef. The treble clef (the curly G sign) is for higher notes. The bass clef is for lower notes. In the treble clef the lines, from the bottom, are E G B D F, and the spaces are F A C E.

Extra short lines called ledger lines extend the staff. Middle C sits on a ledger line just below the treble staff. The shape of the note head tells how long it lasts, which we study in the next stage.

example.q: Which note names are on the spaces of the treble staff, from the bottom?
steps: Spaces are counted from the bottom up.
They spell F, A, C, E.
So the first space is F, then A, C, E.

analogies.home: A bookshelf with five shelves: where a book sits shows which shelf. Notes work the same way.
analogies.city: Floors of an apartment block: higher floor means higher sound.
analogies.nature: Birds on five wires: higher wire, higher note.
analogies.tech: A graph has height for pitch and time along the side.

stages.mnemonic: Lines: Every Good Boy Does Fine. Spaces spell FACE.
terms: Five lines and four spaces on which notes are written.
The sign at the start of the staff that fixes which lines are which notes.
The clef for higher notes, curling around the line G.
A short extra line above or below the staff.

misc.wrong: A note further to the right is higher.
misc.right: Up and down on the staff shows pitch. Left to right shows time.

panel.why: Standard notation uses a five-line staff.

panel.model: Lines can be remembered with Every Good Boy Does Fine (E G B D F) and the spaces simply spell FACE.
panel.why: Memory aids turn the pattern into something easy to recall.

panel.q: Why do composers use ledger lines?

To write notes above or below the staff

To show the tempo of the music
panel.why: Ledger lines extend the staff when notes are too high or low.

teach.model: Music is written on a staff of five lines. The higher a note sits, the higher it sounds. A clef at the start tells us the note names. In treble clef the lines are E G B D F and the spaces spell FACE.

stages.title: Rhythm values
stages.hook: Some notes are long and some are short. How could you write down how long each one lasts?
explain: The shape of a note tells how long it lasts, counted in beats. In common time a quarter note lasts 1 beat, a half note 2 beats and a whole note 4 beats. An eighth note lasts half a beat, so two eighth notes fit into one beat.

Each value is half of the one before it: a whole note equals two halves, a half equals two quarters, and a quarter equals two eighths. A dot after a note adds half of its own value, so a dotted half note lasts 3 beats.
Silence is written too. A rest is a sign for a pause, and each note value has a matching rest. Rests are part of rhythm, because the gaps shape the pattern.

example.q: In 4/4, how many beats are in half note + quarter note + quarter note?
steps: Half note = 2 beats.
Quarter = 1 beat, twice makes 2 beats.

analogies.home: A cake cut in halves, quarters, eighths: the pieces get smaller but make the whole.
analogies.farm: A bucket of 4 litres split into equal jugs shows whole, half and quarter.
analogies.sport: A race of 4 laps: a half note is 2 laps, a quarter 1 lap.
analogies.music: Clapping slowly once for a whole note and four times for four quarters fills the same time.

A note lasting two beats in 4/4.
A note lasting four beats in 4/4.
A sign for a silence of a certain length.

misc.wrong: A half note lasts half a beat.
misc.right: A half note is half of a whole note, so it lasts two beats in 4/4. The eighth note is the one lasting half a beat.

panel.q: Which is true about two quarter notes and one half note?
panel.why: 1 + 1 = 2 beats, the same as a half note.

panel.model: No. A dot adds half the note's own value. For a half note that is 1 beat; for a quarter note it is half a beat.

teach.model: Each note shape lasts a certain number of beats. In 4/4 a quarter note is one beat, a half note is two and a whole note is four. An eighth note is half a beat. Rests show silence of the same lengths.

stages.title: Time signatures
stages.hook: Why can you march to some songs and waltz to others? What changes in the counting?
explain: A time signature is two numbers at the start of the music. The top number says how many beats are in each bar (a bar is one measure between two vertical bar lines). The bottom number says which note value counts as one beat: 4 means quarter note.

So 4/4 has four quarter-note beats in a bar and is often called common time. 3/4 has three beats, which feels like a waltz: ONE-two-three. 2/4 has two beats, like a march. The first beat of a bar is usually the strongest.

Other signatures such as 6/8 count six eighth notes, usually felt in two groups of three, giving a rolling swing. Many songs from around the world use these metres, and some music uses odd numbers such as 5 or 7 beats.

example.q: A bar of 3/4 is filled with quarter notes. How many?
steps: Top number 3 means three beats per bar.
Bottom 4 means a quarter note is one beat.
So three quarter notes fill the bar.

analogies.sport: Rowing strokes can count 1-2 together, like 2/4.
analogies.farm: A rocking chair in six small rocks, grouped in two big ones: like 6/8.
analogies.city: Walking steps are in 2s; skipping feels in 3s.

stages.mnemonic: Top is how many, bottom is which kind.
terms: One group of beats between two bar lines.
Two numbers showing beats per bar and the note that gets a beat.
The pattern of strong and weak beats.

misc.wrong: The bottom number is the number of beats.
misc.right: The top number is the number of beats. The bottom number only says which note value is one beat.

questions.why: Three counts per bar: ONE-two-three.

questions.why: The top number is 2.

teach.model: A time signature has two numbers. The top says how many beats are in each bar. The bottom says which note counts as a beat. So 3/4 has three quarter-note beats and sounds like a waltz.

stages.title: Major and minor scales
stages.hook: Why do some tunes sound bright and cheerful while others sound dark or sad?
explain: A scale is a ladder of notes in order from low to high. The major scale is made from a pattern of whole steps (W, two semitones) and half steps (H, one semitone): W W H W W W H. Starting on C and playing only white keys gives C D E F G A B C.

The natural minor scale uses a different pattern: W H W W H W W. Played from A on the white keys it gives A B C D E F G A. The third note is lower than in major, which gives a darker or more serious colour.

Major often sounds bright and minor darker, but this is a tendency, not a law. Many cultures use other scales as well, such as five-note pentatonic scales found in music from East Asia, Africa, the Americas and Europe.

example.q: Build a C major scale by following W W H W W W H.
steps: Start on C. Whole step up is D.
Whole step to E; half step to F.
Then W to G, W to A, W to B, H to C.
example.a: C D E F G A B C

analogies.home: A staircase with same-height steps but one place with a short step: that short step makes the shape.
analogies.nature: Hills with a pattern of steep and gentle slopes make a skyline like a scale.
analogies.city: A road with pattern of long and short blocks.
analogies.music: Major and minor are like sunny and cloudy: both useful.

stages.mnemonic: Major: Whole Whole Half, Whole Whole Whole Half.
terms: A set of notes in order from low to high.

misc.right: Minor often sounds darker but many happy or energetic songs are in minor too.

stages.limits: The bright-major and dark-minor link is partly learned from culture, not a universal rule.

panel.why: Starting elsewhere changes where the half steps fall.

panel.q: Why do pentatonic scales appear in so many parts of the world?
panel.model: With only five notes, most notes sound pleasant together, so pentatonic scales are easy to sing and play. Many cultures developed them independently.
panel.why: Few notes means fewer harsh intervals.

panel.q: A tune has a half step between its 3rd and 4th notes and its 7th and 8th. What type of scale is it?
panel.why: Major has half steps at those places.

teach.model: A scale is a set of notes in order. The major scale uses the steps whole whole half whole whole whole half and sounds bright. The natural minor scale uses a different pattern and often sounds darker.

stages.title: Basic intervals
stages.hook: Two notes can be close like neighbours or far like cousins. How could we measure the gap between them?
explain: An interval is the distance in pitch between two notes. We count it in semitones for exact size, and we name it by counting letter names including both ends. C up to E is a third because C D E are three letters.
Some common intervals from C: C to D is a second (2 semitones), to E a major third (4), to F a fourth (5), to G a perfect fifth (7), and to the next C an octave (12). A minor third is 3 semitones.
Intervals have colours. Seconds feel close, thirds sweet, perfect fifths strong and open, and octaves very smooth. Songs often start with a famous interval, which helps ear training.

example.q: How many semitones from C (60) to G (67), and what is the interval?
steps: Subtract: 67 − 60 = 7 semitones.
Count the letters C D E F G: five.
Seven semitones over five letters is a perfect fifth.

analogies.home: Steps on stairs: a step, two steps, a whole flight.
analogies.city: Bus stops along a line: the distance between stops is the interval.
analogies.nature: Stepping stones across a stream, some close, some far.

stages.mnemonic: Count the letters; count the semitones.

misc.wrong: A bigger number means exactly the same size every time.
misc.right: Size also depends on semitones. A third can be 3 or 4 semitones: minor or major.

panel.why: An octave is 12 semitones.

teach.model: An interval is the distance between two notes. We name it by counting letters and measure it in semitones. From C, E is a major third, G is a perfect fifth and the next C is an octave.

stages.title: Chords and harmony
stages.hook: When three notes play together, why do they sometimes blend and sometimes clash?
explain: Harmony means notes sounding at the same time. A chord is three or more notes played together. The simplest chord is a triad, built by stacking thirds: a root note, a third above it and a fifth above it.

A major triad has a major third and then a minor third: C E G, which is 4 and then 3 semitones. A minor triad swaps this: C E♭ G, which is 3 then 4 semitones. Major chords sound bright and minor chords sound darker.
Songs from many cultures use chords to support the melody. Guitar strumming and piano accompaniment are common ways to play them.

example.q: Build a C major triad from C by stacking a major third and then a minor third.
steps: Start on C (60).
Major third: add 4 semitones gives E (64).
Minor third: add 3 gives G (67).

analogies.home: Three voices singing different notes at once, like a family choir.

analogies.music: A melody is one voice; a chord is a group of voices.

o: One long note held on its own

questions.why: A chord is notes played at once.

questions.q: Explain why chords support a melody in a song.
questions.model: The chords sound underneath the melody, adding fuller sound and mood so the tune feels grounded.
questions.why: Chords provide harmony and mood for the tune.

panel.q: Why does changing one note of a triad by a semitone change the mood?
o: It changes the third, which decides major or minor
It changes the beat of the music

panel.q: Why might two notes that are a semitone apart sound tense when played together?
panel.model: The two pitches are so close that their sound waves interfere and rub against each other, which our ears hear as tension.
panel.why: Close frequencies cause roughness.

stages.title: Instrument families
stages.hook: An orchestra has dozens of instruments. How do musicians sort them into groups?
explain: Instruments are grouped into families by how they make sound. In a symphony orchestra there are four main families: strings, woodwind, brass and percussion.

Strings (violin, viola, cello, double bass, harp) make sound from vibrating strings. Woodwinds (flute, oboe, clarinet, bassoon) make sound with air across an opening or a reed. Brass (trumpet, horn, trombone, tuba) make sound when the player buzzes the lips into a metal mouthpiece. Percussion (timpani, snare drum, xylophone, cymbals) make sound by being hit or shaken.

Families are about how the sound is made, not what the instrument is made from. A saxophone is made of metal but is woodwind because it uses a reed. Every culture has its own instruments: the kora in West Africa is a string instrument, the sitar in India, the koto in Japan.

example.q: Which family does a clarinet belong to?

panel.q: A student says a flute must be brass because many flutes are made of metal. What is the best reply?

Families depend on how the sound is made, and a flute is blown across an opening

panel.why: Material does not decide the family. Brass instruments are played by buzzing the lips; a flute uses a stream of air across an edge.

teach.model: Instruments are grouped by how they make sound. Strings are plucked or bowed, woodwinds are blown across an opening or reed, brass are buzzed with the lips, and percussion are hit or shaken. An orchestra uses them together.

stages.title: Introductory instrumental performance
stages.hook: You are about to play a short tune for friends. What should you do before, during and after?
explain: Good performance starts with preparing: sit or stand with a relaxed back, hold the instrument properly, and warm up gently. Practise slowly first, then speed up. Short practice every day works better than one long session.

During the performance, keep a steady beat, breathe, and listen to yourself and others. If you make a mistake, keep going. The audience will follow your confidence. When playing in a group, watch for a starting signal and match your volume to the others.
After a performance, take a bow, thank the audience and think about what went well and what to improve. Every culture has a form of performance, from village drumming circles to concert halls.
